newsitem.title: DUBAI: Domestic agenda, not foreign policy, Iran priority.
newsitem.headline: Domestic agenda, not foreign policy, Iran priority.

text.p: Iran's new president Mohammad Khatami assumes office on Sunday facing a heavy domestic agenda which is expected to take priority over any moves towards easing tensions with the West.

The 54-year-old Shi'ite Moslem clergyman, a moderate with a reputation for tolerance compared with many of the conservative clerics who dominate Iranian politics, was elected in May by a surprise landslide.
He succeeds Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, president since 1989, when Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei officially confirms his presidency on Sunday.
The following day Khatami will take the oath of office in a ceremony in the Majlis at which he will also submit his cabinet for parliamentary approval.

His triumph at the head of a curious coalition of supporters rode the crest of a wave of popular resentment with the rigours of Islamic fundamentalism and restrictions ranging from a rigid dress code for women to a ban on satellite television dishes.
After 18 years of revolution since the overthrow of the U.S.-backed Shah, it marked a seismic shift in Iranian politics.

Khatami's main concern is how to satisfy the expectations of the two out of every three voters who enabled him to overwhelm the favoured candidate, conservative parliamentary speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, analysts said on Wednesday.
For most Iranians, that means jobs and economic development, with a renewed attack on inflation that was halved to 23.2 percent in the last full Iranian year to March.

Relations with Washington, where the Clinton administration is being urged to rethink its hostility and engage the largest power in the volatile oil-rich Gulf, and with the European Union can be relegated for a while, the analysts said.
Khatami's victory symbolised the agenda of Iran's youth and therefore their expectations needed to be addressed, the government-owned newspaper Iran Daily said this week.
Issues like better schools, more recreational facilities and above all jobs were on the minds of the youth, it said, adding: "Iran's younger generation deserves the best."
While the focus is on domestic concerns, analysts caution against expecting any sudden switch in the Islamic republic's foreign posture.

"It would be unwise to expect any dramatic changes, particularly in foreign relations," said Rosemary Hollis, head of the Middle East programme at the London-based Royal Institute for International Affairs.
"I think that, for the time being, his election victory is much more about internal developments in Iran which would only secondarily have an influence on foreign relations."
Top of the domestic concerns are high prices, unemployment officially put at 10 percent but believed by diplomats in Tehran to be at least double that, and the need to boost the economy.
"There is a honeymoon period, but he's going to be under scrutiny and pleasing some of those who voted for him may antagonise those who voted for the speaker," Hollis said.

"There will be a bit of regrouping. His allies have got to consolidate their positions. The best thing they could do is deliver something uncontentious like jobs and an economic upturn, and then get on to the more contentious issues like, 'Is there too much corruption?', 'How does it work?', 'Who does it benefit?', and 'How should be it stopped?'"
Hollis said Khatami represented a tide of the future. "The new phase of revolution is more than hinted at but he's not home and dry," she said.
How much leeway Khatami is allowed in order to calm stormy relations with the West remains to be tested.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Tuesday cautioned against reading too much into the Clinton administration's decision not to oppose Iran's first big international energy project since the revolution.

The project is a 2,000 mile (3,200 km) pipeline that would earn Iran hard currency transit fees for natural gas from Turkmenistan on the eastern shore of the Caspian Sea through northern Iran to Turkey and eventually to customers in Europe.
U.S. sanctions which have yet to be enforced aim to isolate Iran for funding international "terrorism", seeking weapons of mass destruction and undermining the Middle East peace process.

They have had a side-effect unwelcome to U.S. business -- isolation from trade opportunities in the growing markets of the oil- and gas-rich Moslem republics of the former Soviet Union in Central Asia and the Caucasus through the gateway of Iran.

Iran denies involvement in "terrorism", says its interest in nuclear technology is for peaceful purposes, and acknowledges its opposition to the U.S.-brokered peace process between Israel and the Palestinians.
